strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored problem: inserting physically plausible, scene-interacting dynamic weather effects (snow, rain, fog, sandstorm) into reconstructed static 3DGS scenes, going beyond object-centric physics methods (PhysGaussian, Feature Splatting) and static weather editing (ClimateNeRF).

The three-stage pipeline (Gaussian-to-particle mapping, MPM simulation with 'stationary' static particles, particle-to-Gaussian transformation) is clearly described, and the effect-specific collision handling (surface projection for snow accumulation, 3D wetness grid with exponential decay for rain, anisotropic accumulation for sandstorms) is a thoughtful engineering contribution that demonstrably improves interaction realism (Fig. 7 ablation).
The framework is versatile: beyond weather, it handles falling/landing objects, and controllability over effect parameters (color, scale, particle quantity) is shown (Fig. 4).

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: the appendix provides implementation details (grid resolution 64^3, TSDF settings, Taichi/feature-splatting codebase), per-effect physical and appearance parameters, baseline code links, and runtime (7 FPS on an RTX A5000).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core pipeline closely follows existing work: PhysGaussian/Feature Splatting already couple MPM with 3DGS (the paper builds directly on the Feature Splatting code), and mesh extraction via 2DGS-style TSDF fusion is standard. The genuinely new elements are the stationary-particle treatment, active particle tracking (a simple thresholding rule, Eq. 3), and hand-crafted per-effect collision/appearance heuristics (manual offsets, scales, colors, and per-scene manual tuning), which are engineering refinements rather than substantive methodological advances.

The evaluation does not support the claim of 'significant improvements' over existing approaches. The only baselines are static editors (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl), which address a fundamentally different task; the authors themselves argue physics-based methods (PhysGaussian, Feature Splatting) and 4D generation methods are not comparable, yet the RainyGS comparison is deferred as 'concurrent' without any discussion of expected differences. The quantitative margins are marginal (e.g., CLIPSim 0.26 vs 0.25, CLIPDir 0.10 vs 0.08), within what is likely metric noise, with no variance, no per-scene breakdown, and an unexplained asterisk marking ClimateNeRF's CLIPSim/CLIPDir values.

There is no user study or perceptual evaluation, which is the standard way to substantiate claims of superior 'visual quality and physical realism' for generative/editing systems of this type. The ablation study covers only collision handling and is purely qualitative; other components (e.g., stationary particles vs. mesh-only collision, the wetness grid) are not ablated.

Appearance parameters are manually specified per scene and per effect, and object appearances come from GaussianDreamer with no mechanism to match the source scene's style. The authors acknowledge this, but it substantially limits the practical utility and scalability of the system, and it is unclear how much of the visual quality is attributable to the physics framework versus hand-tuned rendering parameters.

Physical plausibility is asserted but not measured: MPM parameters (Young's modulus, Poisson ratio) are ad hoc, the rain/fog/snow setups use essentially arbitrary material constants, and no validation against reference footage or physics-based metrics is provided. Several effects (fog with 0.5 gravity drift, keyframed rigid trajectories for drones/UFO/bee) are arguably not physically simulated at all, which weakens the framing of 'physically-based global dynamic effects.'

Quantitative results are reported over only a small set of scenes (five) and aggregate across effects, and key evidence (temporal dynamics, rainfall) is deferred to a project webpage that reviewers cannot verify from the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored application: inserting physically-based, dynamic, global weather effects (snow, rain, fog, sandstorm) into reconstructed static 3DGS scenes, complementing prior object-centric physics methods (PhysGaussian, Feature Splatting) and static weather editors (ClimateNeRF).

The pipeline is complete and well documented: Gaussian-to-particle mapping, MPM simulation with a 'stationary' material for the static scene, active-particle tracking for efficiency, and effect-specific collision handling (surface projection for snow/sand, wetness grid for rain). Appendix A gives enough implementation detail (grid resolution, material parameters, runtime of 7 FPS on an A5000) to support reproducibility.

The system is controllable (effect color, scale, particle quantity), and the demonstrations extend beyond weather to falling objects (leaves, feathers, drone, bee, UFO), showing versatility of the single framework.
The ablation on collision handling (Fig. 7) reasonably demonstrates that the specialized collision techniques are necessary for plausible accumulation.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method 'significantly outperforms existing approaches' is not supported by the evidence. Table 1 compares only against static 3D editing methods (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl) that are fundamentally incapable of dynamic effects, and the metric margins are marginal (CLIPSim 0.26 vs 0.25, CLIPDir 0.10 vs 0.08, VQAScore 0.89 vs 0.87 for ClimateNeRF on F+S). No user study or perceptual evaluation is provided, which is the standard way to validate visual/physical realism for dynamic effects.

The chosen baselines are apples-to-oranges. The relevant dynamic competitors identified by the authors themselves — RainyGS (concurrent rain synthesis), Gaussian Splashing (PBD fluids/solids), AutoVFX — receive at most qualitative comparisons (AutoVFX only, on single-object effects). A rigorous comparison to at least one physics-based dynamic baseline is missing, making the 'state-of-the-art' contribution claim weak.

The core technical machinery is largely assembled from existing components: MPM simulation with rotation-only updates follows PhysGaussian/Feature Splatting directly (the simulation code is built on Feature Splatting's codebase), mesh extraction follows 2DGS/TSDF, and object appearance uses off-the-shelf GaussianDreamer. The remaining novelty — stationary particles, active-particle culling (Eq. 3), and hand-crafted collision heuristics (surface projection offsets, wetness grid decay) — is engineering-level rather than a substantive methodological advance.

Appearance parameters are manually hand-tuned per scene and per effect (Appendix A.3 lists bespoke scales, opacities, and colors for each scene/effect combination), which undermines generality, scalability, and fair comparison; the authors acknowledge this but it is a material limitation, since the reported quality depends on per-scene manual effort unavailable to baselines.

The 'physically plausible' claim is never validated against ground truth. Simulations are run in a normalized unit cube on a coarse 64^3 MPM grid with elastic-like material parameters (e.g., Young's modulus 0.14, Poisson ratio 0.2 for snow) tuned for visual effect rather than validated physics; no comparison to real captured weather footage or any quantitative physical fidelity metric is provided.

Effect fidelity itself appears limited in the static figures: snow renders as dense white speckling that obscures the scene (Figs. 1, 9), rainfall is admittedly 'challenging to visualize', and fog reduces to a uniform wash. Whether these effects hold up under motion is deferred entirely to an external project webpage, which a reviewer cannot fully verify from the manuscript.

Several presentation issues reduce polish: inconsistent metric notation (Table 1 uses a star annotation on ClimateNeRF values that is never explained), typos ('controllabilty', 'collison', 'inputing', 'Sandtorm', 'predfined', 'photrealistic'), and reference duplication ([40] and [41] are the same PhysGaussian paper).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: prior physics-NeRF/3DGS works (PhysGaussian, Feature Splatting, Gaussian Splashing) are object-centric, and this is one of the first frameworks to couple MPM simulation with global, scene-wide dynamic effects in static 3DGS scenes.

The three-stage pipeline (Gaussian-to-particle mapping, MPM simulation, particle-to-Gaussian transformation) is clearly described, and the mesh-based collision handling plus effect-specific refinements (snow surface projection, rainfall wetness grid, sand anisotropic scaling) are sensible, practical contributions with a supporting ablation (Fig. 7).

Good breadth of demonstration: four weather effects plus object-level dynamics (leaves, feather, drone, bee, UFO) across five real-world scenes, with controllability results (Fig. 4) showing users can tune color, scale, and particle quantity.

Reproducibility support is above average: the appendix provides concrete hyperparameters per effect (Young's modulus, Poisson ratio, emission rates, appearance parameters), implementation details including grid resolution and runtime (7 FPS on a single RTX A5000), and links to all baseline codebases used.
Honest limitations section that correctly identifies the lack of bidirectional interaction and the manual/text-to-3D-dependent appearance parameters.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is weak and arguably unfair: the compared methods (ClimateNeRF, GaussCtrl) are static 3D editing techniques that cannot produce dynamics by design, so Table 1 mostly confirms that adding dynamic particles changes the appearance more than text-guided static editing does. The margins are tiny (e.g., CLIPSim 0.26 vs 0.25; CLIPDir 0.10 vs 0.08-0.09), and no significance analysis, per-scene breakdown, timestep-averaging protocol, or user study is provided. Physically-based baselines (PhysGaussian, Gaussian Splashing) and AutoVFX are dismissed without quantitative comparison, weakening the 'significantly outperforms existing approaches' claim.

A material inconsistency undermines the physical-plausibility narrative: Appendix A.3 states that rigid object effects 'follow precisely controlled trajectories defined by keyframes' with interpolated velocities — i.e., the drone, feather, UFO, and bee results are not physically simulated at all, despite Fig. 5/Fig. 8 captions claiming 'physically plausible motion' and the method being positioned as physics-based. Similarly, fog is simulated as 5000 water particles with near-zero gravity, which is a stylized recipe rather than a physically grounded fog model.

The appearance stage is largely manual and per-scene: opacity, scale, and color are 'defined manually on a scene and effect specific basis' (Appendix A.1), which limits generality and means visual quality depends on hand-tuned parameters rather than a learned or automatic process. The paper acknowledges this but it is a substantive methodological limitation, not just a presentation issue.

Novelty is incremental: the core simulation machinery (MPM via Taichi, rotation extraction from the deformation gradient, Gaussian-particle mapping) is directly built on PhysGaussian and Feature Splatting code, and mesh extraction follows 2DGS. The genuinely new elements are the stationary-particle obstacle scheme, active particle culling (Eq. 3), and effect-specific collision handling, which are useful but modest technical contributions.

The rotation update derivation is under-specified: R_i(t) = V U^T from the SVD of the deformation gradient is stated with 'slight abuse of notation' and never validated (the polar-decomposition rotation is conventionally U V^T); no analysis of stability or error of this choice is given.

Only qualitative evidence is given for controllability and for the AutoVFX comparison, and dynamic-vs-static comparisons are inherently judged in a setting that favors the proposed method; the fog/sandstorm results in Figs. 3 and 10 appear washed out at large t, suggesting visual quality degrades over long simulations but is not quantified.
